title: John Breckinridge of Cabell's Dale
summary: John Breckinridge brought his family and 25 enslaved people from Virginia to Cabell's Dale near Lexington in 1793, carried Jefferson's secret Kentucky Resolutions through the legislature in 1798, and died Jefferson's attorney general in 1806.
bodyMarkdown:
In April 1793 [John Breckinridge](/people/#john-breckinridge), a Virginia lawyer, stepped off a flatboat in Kentucky with his family and 25 enslaved people. He headed inland toward land north of Lexington and named it Cabell's Dale, after his wife's family. From that farm he did as much as anyone to shape the new state's politics.

## A Virginian looks west

Breckinridge was [born on December 2, 1760, near Staunton in Augusta County, Virginia](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_Breckinridge_%28U.S._Attorney_General%29), into a Scotch-Irish Presbyterian family. He learned surveying from his uncle [William Preston](/people/#william-preston), studied at William & Mary between interruptions of the Revolutionary War, and was admitted to the bar in 1785. That June he married Mary Hopkins "Polly" Cabell.

Virginia's bar was crowded and its good land taken, while his brothers wrote of plentiful land in Kentucky. In 1792 Virginia voters elected him to Congress, but he [resigned without serving a day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Breckinridge_%28U.S._Attorney_General%29) and left for the West in March 1793.

## Building Cabell's Dale

Much of the land was still held by tenant farmers whose leases had not run out. Breckinridge [bought out earlier claimants and traded in Revolutionary War military warrants](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_Breckinridge_%28U.S._Attorney_General%29), building Cabell's Dale to about 2,467 acres, and by 1800 he held roughly 20,000 acres in all. Having watched tobacco wear out Virginia soil, he refused to grow it.

Hemp was his cash crop, and he distilled whiskey and brandy from his own grain. All of it rested on enslaved labor; by his death he held nearly 70 people in bondage.

## The Kentucky Resolutions

Gov. [Isaac Shelby](/people/#isaac-shelby) made him the state's attorney general. He resigned in November 1797 and won a Fayette County seat in the House, where he rewrote a criminal code that carried the death penalty for more than 200 offenses. In 1798 the legislature [abolished it for every crime except first-degree murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Breckinridge_%28U.S._Attorney_General%29).

That summer, on a trip back to Virginia, he received a draft of resolutions against the Alien and Sedition Acts. [Thomas Jefferson](/people/#thomas-jefferson), then vice president, had [written them in secret](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kentucky_and_Virginia_Resolutions). Breckinridge carried them through the General Assembly in November 1798, softening Jefferson's call for nullification. As Speaker the next year he wrote a second set that endorsed it outright. Jefferson's authorship came out only in 1814.

## The 1799 constitution

He opposed calling a new constitutional convention, fearing for his property in land and people. "Where is the difference," he asked, "whether I am robbed of my horse by a highway-man, or of my slave by a set of people called a Convention?" Elected a delegate anyway, he helped write a constitution that [kept the legislature from emancipating anyone without the owner's consent](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_Breckinridge_%28U.S._Attorney_General%29) and denied the vote to free Black men.

## Senate and cabinet

Elected to the U.S. Senate in 1800, he was Jefferson's floor leader and led the repeal of the Judiciary Act of 1801. In August 1805 Jefferson [made him attorney general](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_Breckinridge_%28U.S._Attorney_General%29), the first cabinet officer from the West.

## Kentucky today

He fell ill at Cabell's Dale in 1806 and [died of tuberculosis on December 14, at 46](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Breckinridge_%28U.S._Attorney_General%29). He was buried on the farm and later moved to Lexington Cemetery. His daughter Mary Ann and her husband, David Castleman, took over the farm's horse and mule breeding, and his grandson [John C. Breckinridge](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_C._Breckinridge) became vice president. A state marker at Mount Horeb Presbyterian Church, a congregation [organized at Cabell's Dale in 1827](https://history.ky.gov/markers/mt-horeb-presbyterian-church), stands nearby, and the map pin marks it.
